Title: Have a Furnace Humidifier? Change the Pad Before Winter
Description: Many furnaces have a whole-house humidifier mounted on the ductwork. Inside is a pad (water panel) that slowly fills with mineral crust, and once it's clogged it stops doing much. Most makers suggest replacing it once a heating season. Turn the humidifier off, open the cover, look at the pad and check your model's manual for the right part. Title: Test the Water Pressure at a House Showing (2 Taps at Once)
Description: At a showing, turn on the upstairs shower and a sink at the same time, then flush a toilet. If the flow drops to a trickle, it can point to old or corroded pipes, a supply problem or a pressure issue. Also look under sinks for stains and drips. Write it down and ask your home inspector to look closely. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Check Holiday Light Strings Before You Hang Them
Description: Before the holiday lights go up, plug each string in on the floor and look it over: frayed or pinched wires, cracked or broken sockets, loose connections and bulbs that get very hot. Throw out damaged strings instead of taping them. Outside, use only lights and extension cords marked for outdoor use, and follow the maker's limit on how many strings connect end to end. Title: Don't Pour Turkey Grease Down the Drain (Do This Instead)
Description: Big holiday meals mean a lot of grease, and pouring it down the sink is a classic way to clog a kitchen drain. It cools and sticks inside the pipes and builds up over time. Let fat and grease cool in a can or jar, put a lid on it and throw it in the trash. Scrape plates into the trash before washing, and don't overload the garbage disposal. Title: The Paper Test for Your Fridge Door Seal (Before the Holidays)
Description: The fridge works hardest during the holidays. Check the door gasket: close the door on a sheet of paper in a few spots around the edge and pull it out. You should feel some drag. If it slides out easily, clean the gasket with warm soapy water and try again. If it still doesn't seal, look up the replacement gasket for your model. More easy kitchen checks on Walter's page.

Title: Always Ask to Look in the Attic Before You Buy a House
Description: Many buyers never look in the attic. From the hatch, with a flashlight and without walking on the insulation, look for dark water stains on the roof boards, daylight where it shouldn't be, signs of mold, droppings or nests, and bathroom fans venting into the attic. Your home inspector will look too, so write down what you saw. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: What Temperature Should Your Water Heater Be Set To?
Description: Energy.gov and safety groups commonly suggest setting a home water heater to about 120°F. It's hot enough for most households, uses less energy than higher settings and lowers the risk of scalding, which matters most for young kids and older adults. Find the dial on the tank (or the display on tankless units) and read your manual before you change it. More five-minute checks on Walter's page.

Title: Older Home With a Fireplace? Ask About the Chimney Liner
Description: In many older homes the chimney flue liner is cracked, worn or was never there at all, and you can't see that from the living room. Before the first fire, have a qualified chimney professional inspect the chimney, as NFPA recommends every year. If you're buying, ask when the chimney was last inspected and cleaned. Title: Make a Home Fire Escape Plan — Two Ways Out of Every Room
Description: NFPA recommends every home have a fire escape plan: know two ways out of every room, make sure doors and windows open easily, and pick a meeting spot outside, like a tree or the mailbox. Walk it with everyone who lives there, including guests who stay over the holidays, and practice it. Pair it with working smoke alarms on every level. More home safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: Holiday Cooking Fire Safety — Stay in the Kitchen
Description: NFPA reports that Thanksgiving is the peak day for home cooking fires, and unattended cooking is a leading cause. If you're frying, grilling or boiling, stay in the kitchen. Keep a lid or baking sheet nearby to smother a small pan fire, and never throw water on a grease fire. Keep kids at least three feet from the stove. More home safety tips on Walter's page.

Title: Fireplace Safety Checklist — 6 Checks Before the First Fire
Description: Before you light the first fire of the season: have the chimney inspected (NFPA says once a year), check that the damper opens and closes, put the screen or glass doors in place, burn only dry seasoned wood, keep three feet clear around the hearth, and keep a lidded metal can for ashes, stored outside away from the house. Title: Furnace Not Turning On? Check This Switch Before You Call
Description: If the furnace won't come on, check the simple things before you call for service: the thermostat is set to heat and has batteries, the furnace filter isn't clogged, the breaker hasn't tripped, and the service switch near the furnace (it looks like a light switch) is on. If it still won't run, or you smell gas, call a heating pro or your gas company. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Buying a House With a Finished Basement or Addition? Ask About Permits
Description: A finished basement, an addition, a new deck or a remodeled kitchen can be a big plus, but ask if the work had permits and passed final inspection. Unpermitted work isn't always bad work, but nobody checked it, and it can cause trouble when you sell or insure the home. Your agent can help you look up permit records with the local building department. More seller questions on Walter's page.

Title: Radiator Cold at the Top? How Bleeding Works in an Older Home
Description: Many older homes heat with hot water radiators. If a radiator is warm at the bottom but cold at the top, trapped air is a common cause. With the system cool, open the small bleed valve with a radiator key, hold a cup and a rag under it, and close it once water comes out. Steam radiators work differently, so check your system first or ask a heating pro. Pick your build year in Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: Traveling for the Holidays? Don't Turn Off the Heat
Description: Going away for the holidays in cold weather? Leave the heat on, set no lower than about 55°F (the American Red Cross suggests this to help prevent frozen pipes). Know where the main water shutoff is, open cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls before a hard freeze, and ask a neighbor to check the house. Title: Winter Power Outage Checklist — What to Have Ready
Description: When the power goes out in winter, most furnaces stop too. Get ready now: flashlights instead of candles, a battery radio and phone power bank, water and food that needs no cooking, blankets for one warm room, CO alarms with battery backup, and a tagged main water shutoff. Never heat the house with the oven, a grill or a generator. Read Walter's full winter outage guide.

Title: How Old Are Your Smoke Alarms? Check the Date on the Back
Description: Smoke alarms don't last forever. NFPA recommends replacing them 10 years from the date of manufacture, which is printed on the back. Carbon monoxide alarms also have a set life; check the label or manual, and many chirp at end of life. Twist each alarm down, read the date, and write a replacement reminder in your calendar. Title: Diagonal Drywall Cracks Above Doors — When to Ask Questions
Description: Look at the corners above doors and windows when you tour a house. Tiny hairline cracks in drywall are common as houses settle and dry out. Wider cracks, cracks that run on a diagonal from the corners, many of them, or doors that also stick can point to movement worth a closer look. Point them out to your home inspector, who may suggest a structural engineer. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Older Home? Close the Storm Windows Before Winter
Description: Many older homes have single-pane windows with storm windows outside them. Before winter, slide the storm panels down, make sure they close fully and check the screens are stored. Look for the small weep holes at the bottom of the frame and keep them clear so water can drain out. Cracked glass or loose frames are worth fixing before the cold. Title: Keep Snow and Ice Off Your Gas Meter and Vents This Winter
Description: After snow or ice, gas companies often ask homeowners to keep the gas meter and the furnace and water heater vents clear. Brush snow off the meter gently by hand or with a broom, never kick it or chip ice with a shovel, and don't pile plowed snow on it. If you ever smell gas, get everyone out and call the gas company from outside. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: 5 Quick House Checks After the First Snow
Description: After the first real snow of the season, take a slow walk around the house: make sure the furnace and water heater vent pipes are clear, brush snow off the gas meter, look for big icicles at the gutters (a possible ice dam sign), make steps and walkways safe, and check that downspouts aren't buried. Do it all from the ground. Get Walter's free Weekend Home Check on his page.
